title: Multi-GPU parallelism: tensor+pipeline benchmarks & NCCL/interconnect investigations (WIP)
content:
Objective:
- Understand performance characteristics and bottlenecks for multi-GPU serving of large transformer models using tensor and pipeline parallelism.
- Quantify scaling (1->8 GPUs), interconnect limits (NVLink vs PCIe vs IB), and NCCL configuration effects on throughput (tokens/sec) and tail latency (p95/p99).
- Produce actionable tuning guidance for production serving configurations (hosted and dedicated clusters).

Scope / quick summary (high level):
- Testbed: DGX-A100 (8x A100 80GB) and 2x 4-GPU nodes connected via Mellanox HDR100 (or 200 where noted). Mixed intra-node (NVLink) and inter-node (IB over HDR) experiments.
- Parallelism modes: pure tensor-parallel (Megatron-style) for single stage, pipeline-parallelism (model parallel with micro-batching) for multi-stage, and combined tensor+pipeline.
- Workloads: production-ish inference requests with typical sequence lengths (32/128/512) and batch sizes tuned for latency SLOs (1-16). Also long-sequence throughput tests for microbenchmarks.
- Tools: nccl-tests (all_reduce/all_gather/alltoall), PyTorch Distributed microbenchmarks, Megatron/DeepSpeed inference harness, nsys/nvprof for GPU timelines, nvtop and nvidia-smi for utilization snapshots, ibv_* tests for IB verification, tcpdump for NIC-level sanity.

Background / motivation (notes):
- Serving runtime must support consistent latency SLOs while maximizing token throughput. Multi-GPU is necessary for large models (>=30B) where KV cache growth and compute exceed a single GPU.
- Two main patterns used in our stack: tensor-parallel to split compute of linear layers across GPUs; pipeline-parallel to split layers across pipeline stages and increase batch-parallel throughput. Each has different communication patterns and sensitivities to interconnect bandwidth/latency.

Testbed details (exact configs used in runs below):
- DGX-A100 (single-node) : 8x NVIDIA A100 80GB, NVLink 3 interconnect, Ubuntu 20.04, CUDA 11.8, NCCL 2.15, PyTorch 2.1.
- Multi-node cluster: 2x nodes, each 4x A100 (40/80GB mix), Mellanox HDR100 IB, RoCE/TCP fallback enabled on some experiments.
- Kernel and driver notes: mlx5 driver v5.x, OFED stack installed. Some runs repeated after driver upgrade to validate changes.
- Software stack: our inference runtime (branch: experiments/multi-gpu-bench), DeepSpeed/transformer-harness for pipeline/tensor scheduling, nccl-tests v2.12 build.

Methodology / measurement approach:
- Small-message vs large-message characterization. Run nccl-tests across message sizes [256B, 1KB, 4KB, 64KB, 512KB, 2MB, 8MB] to map bandwidth/latency knee points.
- Real inference runs instrumented with NVTX markers and nsys capture to measure overlap between compute and NCCL collectives and to see serialization hotspots.
- GPU counters: SM utilization, DRAM throughput, L2 hit/miss, PCIe utilization (when cross-node or when NVLink disabled).
- Repeated runs (>=5) to capture variance and p95/p99 tail latency. Keep node thermal state consistent: cool-down period between runs to avoid thermal throttling artifacts.

Experiments and findings (draft notes / raw observations):
1) Intra-node scaling (1->8 GPUs, NVLink):
   - Throughput scaling for tensor-parallel-only workloads is near-linear up to 4 GPUs; beyond 4 GPUs benefits taper due to increased collectives (all_reduce) overhead and smaller per-GPU work.
   - NVLink fabric provides high aggregate BW; for large messages (>=512KB) we saturate link and see close to theoretical multi-link BW.
   - Observed issue: small-tensor workloads (micro-batch for low-latency requests) are latency-bound. Allreduce latency dominates when message sizes are <4KB. Result: p99 latency inflates even if average latency looks fine.
   - Recommendation: for low-latency small-batch serving, prefer fewer tensor partitions and rely more on pipeline parallelism or model sharding that avoids frequent small collectives.

2) Cross-node scaling (inter-node via IB):
   - Cross-node overhead varies from 10% to 40% depending on message size and NCCL tuning.
   - For large messages, IB performs well and the penalty vs intra-node is modest (~10-15% BW loss). For small messages, cross-node p99 latency can be 2-3x worse because of added hop latency and software stack overhead.
   - Observed occasional unexpected latency spikes correlated with concurrent RDMA connection establishment when jobs start; warm-up runs reduce these spikes.

3) NCCL configuration effects (notes from experiments):
   - NCCL envs we exercised: NCCL_DEBUG=INFO, NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME=eth0/ens5f0, NCCL_IB_DISABLE=0/1, NCCL_P2P_LEVEL=NVL or SYS (varies by NCCL version), NCCL_COLLNET_ENABLE.
   - Enabling CollNet/Tree algorithms improves throughput for large-scale all_reduce in our topology but requires extra patching on heterogeneous node counts. Use with caution for mixed GPU counts.
   - Disabling IB (NCCL_IB_DISABLE=1) drops cross-node performance drastically - useful as a diagnostic but not for production.
   - Setting NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME to the management NIC (instead of using RDMA) killed cross-node performance - ensure correct NIC selection.

4) Pipeline parallelism behavior (micro-batching, bubble reduction):
   - Pipeline-parallel increases throughput by overlapping stage compute, but introduces bubbles for small micro-batches. We tried micro-batch sizes [1,2,4,8]. For stable throughput with constrained latency, micro-batch=2 for 4-stage pipeline is a reasonable sweet spot in our tests.
   - Combining tensor and pipeline parallelism: careful placement of tensor partitions within pipeline stages matters - co-locating tensor peers within the same node (NVLink hops) reduced cross-stage traffic and improved p99.

5) Communication/computation overlap and chunking (critical for inference):
   - Chunking the KV cache updates and attention compute to allow NCCL collectives to run on larger contiguous chunks produced better overlap. Small, frequent collectives serialized more and hurt latency.
   - We experimented with overlapping NCCL calls launched from different CUDA streams - yields good gains when correctly synchronized with CUDA events, but increased complexity and occasional c10d race conditions. Needs more integration QA.

6) Profiling highlights (nsys captures):
   - Typical trace shows alternating compute kernels and NCCL all_reduce/all_gather kernels. When overlap is working, NCCL kernels run concurrently with compute kernels on other GPUs.
   - Hotspots: repeated cudaMemcpyAsync calls to host for small tensors (<1KB) create CPU-side scheduling jitter - move to in-GPU buffers where possible.

Representative numbers (rough, experimental, single-node DGX-A100):
- Model X (30B) inference long-run throughput (tokens/sec) at sequence=128:
  - 1 GPU : 16k tokens/s
  - 2 GPU (tensor-parallel 2) : 30k tokens/s (1.9x)
  - 4 GPU (tensor-parallel 4) : 56k tokens/s (3.5x vs 1GPU)
  - 8 GPU (tensor-parallel 8) : 95k tokens/s (6x vs 1GPU) - diminishing returns after 4 GPUs due to smaller per-GPU workload and increased all_reduce overhead.
- Tail latency (p99) for small-batch queries (batch=1, seq=32):
  - 1 GPU : 120ms p99
  - 4 GPU (TP=4) : 260ms p99 (most of extra latency is collective latency)
  - 4 GPU (pipeline 4) : 170ms p99 (better p99 than TP in this case due to fewer small collectives)

Actionable recommendations (draft):
- For low-latency single-request serving (batch sizes 1-4): prefer pipeline-parallel stage placements that minimize cross-node communication. Reduce tensor split factor to keep collective sizes above the small-message knee.
- For throughput-oriented workloads (batching allowed): use larger tensor splits with careful NCCL tuning (enable CollNet/tree for large scales if topology supports it). Use micro-batching to amortize pipeline bubbles.
- NCCL best practices we validated: pin NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME to the correct RDMA NIC, ensure IB firmware/drivers are up-to-date, run nccl-tests during cluster provisioning, and set NCCL_DEBUG=INFO only for debugging (verbose).
- Avoid frequent small host<->device copies for KV cache operations; keep KV buffers resident on GPU and chunk updates where possible.

Open issues / next experiments (todo):
- Re-run key experiments on HDR200 IB to quantify interconnect generation improvements.
- Systematically sweep NCCL_ALGO and P2P_LEVEL knobs (NCCL versions differ; need to test v2.14 vs v2.15 behavior).
- Test heterogeneous node setups (4x + 8x GPU mixed) and validate fallback routing behavior in our runtime when nodes with different counts participate.
- Integrate automated nccl-test runs into CI for each cluster image build so regressions are caught early.

Appendix: commands and snippets (working notes)
- nccl-tests build/run (example):
  git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/nccl-tests.git
  make MPI=1
  mpirun -np 8 --map-by ppr:4:node ./build/all_reduce_perf -b 4 -e 8M -f 2 -g 8

- nsys capture example:
  nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,nccl -o trace_modelX ./run_inference.sh --config configs/modelX_tp4.json

- PyTorch DP/TP/PP debug run (example):
  python -m torch.distributed.run --nproc_per_node=4 --nnodes=2 --node_rank=$RANK scripts/infer.py --model modelX --tp 2 --pp 2 --micro-batch 2

- Quick checks:
  - ibv_devinfo and ibv_rc_pingpong for IB link sanity
  - nvidia-smi topo -m to confirm NVLink topology
  - watch -n 1 "nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,utilization.memory --format=csv"

Notes to self (stylistic / planning):
- Clean up raw numbers, put final runs behind reproducible script with seed and image tag.
- Consolidate perf plots (throughput vs gpus, p99 vs gpus, bytes/sec by message size) and add to confluence page linked above.
- Follow up with SRE to add nccl-tests and ibv checks to node provisioning pipeline.
